strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap: existing diffusion-based intrinsic decomposition methods (RGB↔X, IID, DiffusionRenderer) target indoor/object scenes, while weather-editing methods operate in pixel space without physical interpretability. Framing weather editing as intrinsic-space manipulation is a well-motivated and reasonably novel angle.

The proposed Intrinsic Map-Aware Attention (IMAA) is a concrete, technically interesting mechanism: learnable per-intrinsic-map embeddings with a gating module that constructs attention biases in the DiT, addressing a real observed failure mode (poor handling of distant/small objects and map-specific regions). It is supported by both quantitative ablation (Tab. 3) and qualitative evidence (Fig. 11a).

CLIP-space interpolation of weather prompt embeddings (Eq. 1-2) with feature distillation from the original Stable Diffusion prior is a simple and effective way to obtain continuous weather intensity control, demonstrated convincingly in Fig. 7 (light-to-heavy rain/snow transitions) where WeatherWeaver behaves more like a filter.

The authors construct and promise to release two sizable datasets (WeatherSynthetic, 38k UE5-rendered images with intrinsic maps; WeatherReal, 18k real driving images), addressing the documented lack of outdoor weather-diverse intrinsic datasets. The dataset motivation section thoughtfully discusses why existing options (OpenRooms, Hypersim, MatrixCity, MatrixCity) are inadequate.

Evaluation is fairly comprehensive: comparisons against rendering-based and pixel-space editing baselines (Tabs. 1), weather restoration methods, inverse rendering decomposition quality across five intrinsic maps (Tab. 3), a user study (81.67% preference), and importantly a downstream-task validation showing large detection/segmentation gains on ACDC (AP50 56.56→61.32, mIoU 24.13→30.05), which demonstrates practical utility beyond perceptual metrics.

The limitations section is honest (no temporal consistency guarantee, single-image scope), and the related work clearly positions the contribution relative to WeatherWeaver, IntrinsicEdit, and diffusion rendering methods.
weaknesses: Several core technical details are deferred entirely to supplementary material: the feature distillation implementation, the heuristic-guided progressive training strategy (gradient operator for irradiance, shadow-boundary extraction), and details of the joint attention bias application. The main paper alone is insufficient to assess or reproduce the method.

The claim of 'over 10 dB PSNR improvement in inverse rendering' in the introduction is potentially misleading: against finetuned baselines (the fair comparison, given the authors finetune IID and RGB↔X on their data), the gain in Tab. 3 is ~3.2 dB (29.99 vs 26.78 for RGB↔X w/ finetune). The 10 dB figure appears to rely on non-finetuned baselines.

The forward-rendering comparisons rely heavily on perceptual/no-reference metrics (PickScore, CLIP-S, DINO-S). Notably, Flux-Kontext achieves higher PickScore and DINO-S (83.50 vs 73.63 and 85.50 vs 73.63), and the authors argue these metrics are not appropriate for physical consistency; this argument is qualitative and rests on visual inspection rather than a quantitative measure of geometry/material preservation, which is the paper's central claim.

WeatherReal pseudo-labels are generated by the authors' own inverse renderer (applied to Waymo/Kitti), then used to train the models — a partially circular data pipeline whose quality ceiling is not independently validated; the manual quality-check procedure is described only at a high level.

The user study is small in scope (61 participants, 8 cases), and there is no quantified editing-consistency metric (e.g., background preservation) for the editing task beyond DINO-S, where the method ranks below two baselines.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the paper states datasets will be released but makes no explicit commitment to releasing code, training configurations, or compute details; WeatherReal is 'only used to finetune and not used to evaluate results,' which limits external verification of real-world decomposition quality (the consistency check across weather conditions is relegated to supplementary).

Some writing/consistency issues: Table 1 shows the method ranks second on several PickScore columns behind pixel-space methods, which is under-discussed; the contribution bullet claims 'state-of-the-art' broadly while metric wins are mixed (e.g., Qwen-Image-Edit leads CLIP-S and DINO-S in Tab. 1).

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and the framing is sensible: weather effects are physically tied to illumination rather than intrinsic material properties, so editing weather in an intrinsic (material/geometry/irradiance) space is a principled alternative to pixel-space editing, and the paper positions this against prior work (WeatherWeaver, RGB<->X, DiffusionRenderer, IntrinsicEdit) reasonably well.

The paper is substantial in scope: a weather-aware inverse renderer, a weather-conditioned forward renderer with CLIP-space prompt interpolation for graded weather intensity, an intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) module, and two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic, 38K UE5 renders with intrinsic maps; WeatherReal, 18K real images), with a stated intent to release the data.

Evaluation covers multiple axes: editing vs. pixel-space editors, comparison vs. weather restoration methods, inverse/forward rendering comparisons, ablations of IMAA and of WeatherReal fine-tuning, a small user study, a fine-grained intensity control comparison (Fig. 7), and a downstream evaluation showing detection (AP75 13.15->24.60) and segmentation (mIoU 24.13->30.05) gains on ACDC after weather correction.

The IMAA motivation is supported by observation (Fig. 4 shows different intrinsic maps require attention to different regions), and the ablation in Table 3 (Ours w/o IMAA) shows a measurable degradation across all map types, giving some evidence the module helps.
Fine-grained weather control via alpha interpolation in CLIP space (Fig. 7) is a practical and desirable capability that the closest baseline (WeatherWeaver) demonstrably lacks.
weaknesses: Overstated headline claims vs. the actual numbers. The abstract/intro claim the method 'outperforms state-of-the-art' editing, yet in Table 1 Flux-Kontext achieves much higher DINO-S (85.50 vs. 73.63) — a structural-consistency metric directly aligned with the paper's core selling point of geometry/material preservation — and higher PickScore on sunny scenes. The paper dismisses this metric without a rigorous argument. Similarly, the claimed '>10 dB PSNR improvement' in inverse rendering over all baselines (Table 3, e.g., 27.99 vs. 11.96 for the best fine-tuned baseline) is suspiciously large and needs more careful analysis of baseline configurations to be credible.

Heavy reliance on deferred content: the feature distillation of the forward renderer, the 'heuristic-guided progressive IMAA' training strategy, the gradient operator used to build attention biases, dataset sample inspection, and additional ablations are all relegated to supplementary material. Key technical components of the method are therefore not fully assessable from the manuscript.

The quantitative downstream evaluation (Table 2) only measures the proposed method before/after editing; restoration baselines (AWRaCLE, Histformer), which are qualitatively compared in Fig. 8, are not given the same downstream quantitative treatment, so the claimed superiority for robustness applications is not fully substantiated.

Potential circularity and dataset concerns: WeatherReal is constructed by running Flux-Kontext (a compared baseline) to alter real images, with only manual quality checks; the 'ground truth' for real data is thus generated by an editing model. Additionally, deriving and planning to release data based on Waymo and KITTI raises licensing questions — an issue the paper itself invokes to dismiss MatrixCity.

Evaluation on real data is thin: there is no quantitative inverse-rendering evaluation on real images (only consistency-across-weather PSNR and qualitative Fig. 9), the user study covers only 8 cases, and Table 2's reported detection metrics omit mIoU and segmentation omits mAP entries in a confusing format.

Limited technical novelty of individual components: CLIP prompt interpolation (Eqs. 1–2) is a well-known technique, and IMAA is a relatively simple attention-bias mechanism; the paper's novelty rests largely on the system-level combination and the datasets, which makes rigor of evaluation and completeness of detail all the more important — and both are only partially met. The framework also explicitly does not handle video/temporal consistency (Fig. 12 shows sequences without quantitative consistency evidence), which limits usefulness for the autonomous-driving motivation emphasized throughout.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: moving weather editing from pixel space to intrinsic space, which enables disentanglement of weather-variant illumination from weather-invariant material and geometry — a sensible physical insight for autonomous driving scenes where prior intrinsic-decomposition work (IID, RGB<->X, DiffusionRenderer, IntrinsicEdit) targets indoor scenes or object-level edits.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against both pixel-space editing baselines (Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Instruct-Pix2Pix) and rendering/restoration baselines (RGB<->X, DiffusionRenderer, IID, AWRaCe, Histofomer) across multiple benchmarks (WeatherSynthetic, Waymo, TransWeather, ACDC), with quantitative tables (Tabs. 1-3), qualitative figures, a user study (81.67% preference), and downstream-task validation (detection AP50 13.15->24.60, segmentation mIOU 24.13->30.05 on ACDC), which directly demonstrates practical usefulness rather than only perceptual metrics.

The intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) mechanism is a reasonable, well-placed technical contribution: using DINOv2 patch tokens, learnable map embeddings, and a gating mechanism to construct attention biases that focus the DiT on regions relevant to each intrinsic map is supported by both ablations (Tab. 3 shows consistent metric drops without IMAA) and qualitative evidence (Figs. 3, 11).

The two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic with 38k UE5-rendered images with intrinsic maps, and WeatherReal with 18k real images) address a genuine gap — existing intrinsic datasets (OpenRooms, Hypersim, InteriorVerse) are indoor-only and MatrixCity lacks weather diversity — and their release would benefit the community.

Fine-grained weather control via CLIP-space alpha interpolation (Fig. 7) produces plausible gradual transitions (e.g., progressive snowfall accumulation), which competing pixel-space methods like WeatherWeaver lack.
The paper is honest about limitations (no temporal consistency guarantee for video, single-image scope), which increases credibility.
weaknesses: Key technical details are deferred to the supplementary material, weakening the main paper's self-containedness: the feature distillation implementation, the heuristic-guided progressive training for IMAA, the gradient operator used to extract illumination/shadow boundaries, training losses, and hyperparameters are all not described in the main text. The method section reads at a high level (Eqs. 1-5 cover only the CLIP shift, gating, and attention bias), making it hard to assess technical soundness or reproducibility from the main paper alone.

Potential circularity in the WeatherReal dataset and its use in evaluation: WeatherReal annotations are produced by the authors' own inverse renderer on Waymo/Kitti, with quality controlled by manual checking and a pre-trained Flux-Kontext editing step. The dataset therefore encodes the method's own priors, and using it to finetune both renderers (and to argue generalization, Fig. 11b) makes independent quality assessment difficult; the claimed 18k real images have no ground-truth intrinsic maps.

The physical validity of some intrinsic channels is under-justified: WeatherSynthetic is rendered with UltraDynamic Sky plugins rather than a physically based renderer, and 'metallicity'/'roughness' maps for outdoor driving scenes (Fig. 9) are hard to verify; no quantitative check against UE5's actual material parameters is reported.

Comparison fairness concerns: the strongest editing baselines (Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit) are general-purpose editors rather than weather-specific models, and the paper beats WeatherWeaver partly by construction of the evaluation protocol; also, several baselines in Tab. 1 use 'recommended instruction formats' that may not be equally tuned. Weather-specific generative baselines (e.g., ClimateDiffusion, WeatherGAN-style methods cited in related work) are not compared quantitatively.

Editing metrics (PickScore, CLIP-S, DINO-S) are prompt- and encoder-dependent and do not measure physical consistency of the decomposition; the claimed 'over 10 dB PSNR improvement in inverse rendering' is only verifiable on the synthetic test set where GT maps exist, while consistency across weather on real data (PSNR between maps recovered under different conditions) is deferred to the supplementary material.

Modest novelty of individual components: CLIP embedding-space interpolation and diffusion-based inverse/forward rendering are established ideas; the main novelty is their adaptation to weather editing plus IMAA, which is an attention-bias construction. This is acceptable but the paper could better isolate what is fundamentally new versus engineering.
Fig. 12 shows video sequence results despite Sec. 4.5 explicitly stating the framework does not guarantee temporal consistency; the role of this figure is unclear and risks overclaiming.
Reproducibility hinges on dataset release ('will be released') and supplementary details; training cost, resolution, and inference time are not reported in the main paper.
